sn12.48:1.2: “Cosmology” (_lokāyata_) was a branch of worldly knowledge within regular Vedic studies concerned with the nature and extent of the world and how this may be known ([an9.38](), [sn12.48](); cf. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.3.1). Vedic metaphysics posited “existence” as a primordial “oneness” from which the diversity of the world arises.
sn12.48:2.2: The “oldest cosmology” is a reference to the literal oldest Indian cosmology, the Nāsadīya Sūkta, which begins: “The nonexistent did not exist, nor did the existent exist at that time” (Rig Veda 10.129.1, Jamison/Brereton translation).
sn12.48:4.2: After discussing existence for six lines, the seventh line of the Nāsadīya Sūkta begins, “That One breathed without wind by its independent will. There existed nothing else beyond that.” Then, ”that One was born by the power of heat”.
sn12.48:5.1: _Puthutta_ is used elsewhere of a “spreading” poison, but only here in a philosophical sense. Throughout the Rig Veda _pṛthu_ is used for the “broad” earth or waters, spread out by Indra (eg. 10.113.4) and burned over by Agni (10.156.3). It has sexual connotations, too: a wide womb (10.99.2) or a fat ass (10.86.8; see too Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.2.5.16, 3.5.1.11). This loops back to the Nāsadīya Sūkta, where instead of _pṛthu_ (“broad”) we find _tiraścīna_ (“across”); that the two terms are synonymous is confirmed by ŚB 6.3.3.19 describing the searching minds of the sage-poets: “Their cord was stretched across: Did something exist below it? Did something exist above? There existed placers of semen and there existed greatnesses. There was independent will below, offering above” (10.129.5). “Greatnesses” refers to pregnancy.
